Extremity
ek-STREM-ih-tee
n. (the utmost point, degree, or state; a condition of great distress or peril)
Latin extremitas, from extremus, outermost, the superlative of exter, outward. An extremity is, at root, the outermost point a thing can reach — the edge beyond which there is nothing further of the same kind.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Elihu's speech to Job, in the long dialogue that occupies most of the book, uses the word at a moment of careful theological correction. Job has complained that crying out to God brings no answer; Elihu's response names the actual state of Job's suffering with unusual precision: because it is not so, he hath visited in his anger; yet he knoweth it not in great extremity. The claim is subtle — Elihu does not deny that Job is suffering greatly, but he denies that Job's suffering has actually reached the extremity Job himself imagines it has, and suggests that God's silence is not indifference but a form of restraint even in the midst of real affliction.

Whatever the merits of Elihu's specific diagnosis of Job's case, the passage names something true about how suffering is experienced from the inside: extremity is not merely a matter of the pain actually endured but of how total and inescapable that pain feels to the sufferer in the moment, which is not always the same measurement. Elihu goes on to charge Job with multiplying words without knowledge, precisely because Job's own sense of extremity had begun to outrun the actual facts of his case. Scripture elsewhere is entirely willing to let a sufferer's cry from genuine extremity stand unquestioned, as in many of the Psalms; Elihu's speech is one of the rare places where an extremity claimed is itself weighed and found, in this particular instance, to have been overstated.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the utmost point or degree; the highest degree of distress, danger, or necessity; also, the outermost part.

expand to see more

EXTREMITY, n. The utmost point, degree, or state; the highest degree of distress or need; the outermost part.

VISIT, v.t. To come upon, especially with judgment, affliction, or punishment; also, to go to see.

KNOW, v.t. To perceive with certainty; to have clear and certain understanding of a fact or truth.

MULTIPLY, v.t. To increase in number; to make many; here, of words spoken without corresponding substance.

AFFLICTION, n. A state of pain, distress, or misery; a trial permitted or sent by divine providence.

Key Scripture

Job 35:14 — "Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust thou in him."

Job 35:15 — "But now, because it is not so, he hath visited in his anger; yet he knoweth it not in great extremity:"

Job 35:16 — "Therefore doth Job open his mouth in vain; he multiplieth words without knowledge."

Psa 107:6 — "Then they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses."

Modern Corruption

A sufferer's own sense of reaching an absolute extremity is treated as automatically authoritative and beyond question, when Elihu's speech to Job shows Scripture willing, in at least this one case, to weigh a claimed extremity against the actual facts and find it overstated.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; extremity still names the utmost point of distress. The principle worth recovering is the careful, unusual work Elihu's speech is doing. Most of Scripture's treatment of suffering, especially in the Psalms, takes the sufferer's own cry of extremity at face value and answers it with comfort rather than correction.

Elihu's speech to Job is one of the rare exceptions, and it is worth noting precisely because it is rare: he does not deny Job's real affliction, but he questions whether Job's sense of total abandonment matches what has actually happened, and charges him with multiplying words without knowledge as a result. Psalm 107's own testimony, that those who cried unto the LORD in their trouble were delivered out of their distresses, shows the ordinary pattern extremity is met with in Scripture; Elihu's speech is the harder, more exceptional case of a suffering man's own diagnosis of his extremity being gently, respectfully, but genuinely disputed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew behind Job 35:15's “great extremity” is an intensified idiom rather than a single fixed noun, built on words for visiting in anger and abounding trouble.

expand to see more

Hebrew idiom (Job 35:15) — the verse's “great extremity” renders a Hebrew phrase built on intensity rather than a single fixed noun, underlining how much of the verse's force is Elihu's own interpretive framing.

Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to attend to, often with judgment; the verb behind “he hath visited in his anger.”

Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to multiply, to increase; the verb behind “he multiplieth words without knowledge.”

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice, a legal cause; the standing matter Elihu insists is before God even in silence.

Hebrew tsarah (H6869) — distress, trouble, adversity; the standard word for the affliction Psalm 107:6 describes as met with deliverance.

Usage

"“yet he knoweth it not in great extremity” — Elihu's careful, disputed diagnosis of Job's own claim."

"“he multiplieth words without knowledge” — Elihu's charge against an overstated extremity."

"“they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them” — the ordinary pattern extremity is met with elsewhere."
